title: Exothermic or endothermic? Bond breaking and making
examples: What is the difference between exothermic and endothermic?
Why does breaking bonds take energy?

explain.say: Some reactions make things hot, like a burning match. Others make things cold, like a sports cold pack that turns icy when you squeeze it. Look at the board. You can see the two kinds side by side.

draw.text: Exothermic or endothermic? Bond breaking and making

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Compare energy in and energy out

explain.say: See the left side? Exothermic means heat goes out. The reaction gives energy to the surroundings, so the beaker or your hand warms up. Burning fuel and winter hand warmers are exothermic. Can you think of another reaction that gets hot?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Compare energy in and energy out

explain.say: Now look at the right side. Endothermic means heat goes in. The reaction takes energy from the surroundings, so they cool down. A cold pack works like this, and so does photosynthesis in plants. Where do you think plants get that energy?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Compare energy in and energy out

explain.say: From sunlight! Look at the reasons on the board. Breaking bonds always takes energy in, like pulling magnets apart. Making new bonds always gives energy out, like magnets snapping together. Which do you think wins in a burning match?

explain.say: Making bonds wins, so energy comes out! Great work. If making bonds releases more than breaking takes, it is exothermic; if less, endothermic. Wow: one litre of petrol stores about 34 million joules, enough to lift your family car over 3 kilometres straight up.

faq.a: An exothermic reaction gives out energy, usually as heat, to the surroundings, so the temperature rises. Combustion and neutralisation are exothermic.
An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature falls. Thermal decomposition and photosynthesis are endothermic.

faq.q: Why does breaking bonds take energy?
faq.a: Atoms in a bond are attracted to each other, so you must put in energy to pull them apart. Making the same bond releases the same amount of energy.

faq.q: How do you tell if a reaction is exothermic?
faq.a: Measure the temperature of the surroundings: if it rises, the reaction is exothermic. In bond energy terms, more energy is released making bonds than is taken breaking them.
asks: How do you know if energy is given out?

faq.q: What is an energy profile diagram?
faq.a: It shows the energy of the reactants and products, with a hump for the activation energy. For exothermic reactions the products end lower; for endothermic ones they end higher.
asks: How do you draw an energy level diagram?

facts: Breaking chemical bonds is endothermic; forming bonds is exothermic.
Combustion, neutralisation and respiration are exothermic; photosynthesis and thermal decomposition are endothermic.

quiz.say: A reaction makes the test tube feel cold. What kind of reaction is it?
quiz.show: A reaction makes the test tube feel cold. What kind of reaction is it?
quiz.why: It takes heat in from its surroundings, including your hand.

wrong.1: Exothermic reactions give out heat, so the tube would feel warm.
wrong.2: Feeling cold shows heat was taken in, so it is endothermic.

quiz.say: In an exothermic reaction, which is true?
quiz.show: In an exothermic reaction, which is true?

options.show: Making bonds releases more energy than breaking takes
options.say: Making bonds releases more energy than breaking takes

quiz.why: The energy released by new bonds is bigger, so heat is given out overall.

wrong.0: Breaking bonds always takes energy in.
wrong.1: Bonds in the reactants must break before new ones form.
